title: Radiation from an isolated source
one_line_summary: Outlines Bondi's non-linear treatment of gravitational radiation from an axisymmetric, non-rotating isolated source: null hypersurfaces as characteristic wave fronts, radiation coordinates and the Bondi metric, the characteristic initial value problem, the news function and the exact mass-loss theorem, then surveys the algebraic tools (Petrov types, principal null directions, peeling, optical scalars, Goldberg-Sachs) used to describe radiation invariantly.
role_in_book: The last of the three gravitational-wave chapters. Chapter 21 derived waves and energy flux only in the linearized theory, and Chapter 22 found exact plane and cylindrical waves that have no source. This chapter closes the loop by asking whether a bounded, genuinely non-linear source really loses mass by radiating, and answers yes without any weak-field assumption. It pulls together machinery built much earlier (the Cauchy problem of Ch. 13, the 2+2 formalism of Ch. 14, null hypersurfaces of Ch. 17, Penrose diagrams and null infinity of Ch. 18, null tetrads and mass definitions of Ch. 20) and ends with classification tools and the null Raychaudhuri equation that point towards exact-solution theory and the singularity theorems, before the book turns to cosmology in Ch. 24.

assumed_background.topic: Cauchy problem for the vacuum field equations: evolution equations g^{00} g_{ab,00} = 2M_{ab}, constraints, and their preservation by the contracted Bianchi identities
Condition g^{00} = 0 for x^0 = const to be a null hypersurface; timelike/spacelike/null character of coordinates
Killing vectors, hypersurface-orthogonal symmetries and adapted coordinates
Conformal compactification, Penrose diagrams, future and past null infinity, spatial infinity i^0
2+2 and characteristic decompositions of the metric with lapse and shift
Weyl conformal tensor, its symmetries and its relation to Riemann and Ricci tensors (6.88)
Ricci identity for commuting covariant derivatives and the absolute derivative along a curve
ADM and Komar definitions of mass
Linearized gravitational waves, transverse ring distortion, quadrupole formula and energy flux
Exact plane waves, Einstein-Rosen waves, and singularities from colliding plane waves
Tidal distortion felt by a radially infalling observer in Schwarzschild
Null tetrads and principal null congruences of Kerr
Classification of second-order PDEs as hyperbolic, elliptic, parabolic; characteristics
Sommerfeld outgoing-radiation condition for wave equations
Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and degenerate roots of characteristic polynomials
Asymptotic expansions in inverse powers and big-O notation

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why the linearized quadrupole result leaves open whether gravitational waves really carry energy, and state the quiescent-radiating-quiescent source model used to settle it.

Reader can show that a surface x^0 = const on which the Cauchy evolution equations cannot be solved for second time derivatives must have g^{00} = 0, i.e. is null, and so is a characteristic hypersurface.
Reader can prove that the integral curves of l^a = g^{ab} ∂_b u for a family of null hypersurfaces are null geodesics with affine parameter.
Reader can build radiation coordinates (u, r, θ, φ), derive g^{00} = g^{02} = g^{03} = 0, and explain the difference between Bondi's areal (luminosity) r and the Newman-Penrose affine r.
Reader can write down the Bondi radiating metric, identify its four free functions V, U, β, γ, and say which encode lapse and shift in the 2+2 picture.
Reader can sort the ten vacuum equations into symmetry, main (hypersurface plus dynamical), trivial and supplementary groups and describe the null-cone marching schema.
Reader can list the free data of the characteristic problem (γ on N_0, news on scri+, M and d on the cut) and place them on a Penrose diagram.
Reader can define the news function, mass aspect and Bondi mass, and derive m_{,u} = -½∫ n_{,u}^2 sin θ dθ from the supplementary equation with axis regularity.
Reader can state the Petrov types, arrange them in Penrose's specialization diagram, and relate them to coincidences of principal null directions.
Reader can state the peeling theorem and interpret each order in 1/r as a Petrov type, and describe Szekeres' test-particle pictures for types N, III and D.
Reader can define the expansion, twist and shear of a null geodesic congruence, interpret them via Sachs' shadow picture, and state the Goldberg-Sachs theorem and the null Raychaudhuri equation.

teaching_approach.summary: A compressed research-level survey rather than a full derivation. The authors pose one sharp physical question (does a real, non-linear isolated source lose mass by radiating?), fix a deliberately simple model (axisymmetric, reflection-symmetric, quiescent before and after), and then walk through Bondi's programme step by step, proving only the short geometric lemmas (null hypersurfaces are characteristic, their generators are affinely parametrized null geodesics, coordinate conditions on the metric) while quoting the heavy asymptotic results and delegating derivations to exercises. Pictures carry much of the load: a world-tube diagram states the goal, cone sketches show the coordinates and the marching schema, and a Penrose diagram shows where the free data live. The second half switches from the specific metric to invariant algebra (Petrov, peeling, optical scalars), linking each abstract type to a physical picture of test particles or shadows.
narrative_arc: Motivating doubt: linearized results and source-free exact waves cannot decide whether gravitational waves carry energy away from a real source.

Choose the simplest radiating model: after spherical and two-Killing-vector cases, allow one rotational Killing vector plus azimuthal reflection; state the goal pictorially as a world tube whose mass drops (Fig. 23.1).

Identify wave fronts: hyperbolic equations admit time-bomb solutions carried on characteristics; the Cauchy evolution equations fail exactly when g^{00} = 0, so characteristic surfaces are null hypersurfaces.
Build coordinates on those fronts: u labels null hypersurfaces, their generators are shown to be affinely parametrized null geodesics, r runs along rays, angles label rays at scri+.
Reduce the metric: ray conditions, areal choice of r and the two symmetries collapse g_ab to Bondi's four-function metric, reinterpreted in 2+2 lapse/shift language.

Set up the characteristic initial value problem: group the field equations, state the Bianchi lemma, split main equations into hypersurface and dynamical, and describe marching from one null cone to the next.
Go asymptotic: impose fall-off and an outgoing condition, expand in 1/r, record the free functions, and identify the news as the data that drives evolution; name the BMS group along the way.
Payoff: integrate the exact supplementary equation over angles to obtain the Bondi mass-loss formula and the news theorem; note Sachs' generalization and positivity of Bondi mass.
Change viewpoint to invariants: algebraic classification of the Weyl tensor (Petrov, Penrose diagram, Debever principal null directions), with known solutions assigned to types.
Physical meaning of the algebra: peeling expansion of curvature along outgoing rays and Szekeres' test-particle distortions for types N, III, D.
Close with null congruence kinematics: optical scalars, Sachs' shadow interpretation, Goldberg-Sachs, and the null Raychaudhuri equation as a bridge to the singularity theorems.
signature_moves: States the final theorem pictorially before any mathematics: a hatched world tube narrows between two null cones with m_2 < m_1.
Defines characteristic surfaces operationally as those where the Cauchy data fail to determine second time derivatives, and reuses the book's own evolution equation (13.23) to read off g^{00} = 0.
Short line-by-line covariant proof that null-hypersurface generators are geodesics, pointing to exactly where torsion-freeness and nullness of the whole family are used.
Reduces a general metric to Bondi form by successive coordinate choices and symmetries, each converted into vanishing components, with the algebra pushed into a single guided exercise.
Uses a bookkeeping hierarchy of field equations (symmetry, main, trivial, supplementary; hypersurface vs dynamical) as the organizing structure for an otherwise unreadable calculation.
Counts free data as functions of three, two and one variables and places each on a Penrose diagram, making 'what can you choose freely' visual.
Turns a sign into a theorem: the mass-loss integrand is a square, so mass loss happens exactly when news is non-zero.
Pairs each abstract algebraic type with a concrete physical picture (triangle of specialization, peeling arrows, deformed rings of particles, shadows on a screen).
Frequent parenthetical 'exercise' markers and one open 'why?' prompt to hand verification to the reader.

sections.title: Radiating isolated sources
sections.summary: Argues that neither linearized waves nor global exact wave solutions settle whether gravitational radiation transports energy, because non-linearity matters (colliding plane waves already form singularities) and exact waves lack sources. Proposes studying a bounded source that is static, radiates for a finite time, then settles, and expects its mass to drop. Since spherical sources cannot radiate and two-Killing-vector cases were done in Ch. 22, it adopts Bondi's assumptions: one hypersurface-orthogonal rotational Killing vector with azimuthal reflection invariance (no rotation), optionally equatorial reflection (dropped as unhelpful). It flags, but sets aside, the worry that backscatter might keep the source excited forever.
key_moves: Motivation: energy transfer, not wave existence, is the physical test of whether gravitational waves are radiation like any other.
Model: quiescent for a semi-infinite past, radiating for a finite interval, quiescent again; predicted mass drop drawn as Fig. 23.1.
Symmetry ladder: spherical (no waves) -> two commuting spacelike Killing vectors (Ch. 22) -> one rotational Killing vector plus reflection (Bondi).
Symmetries written as coordinate invariances (23.1)-(23.3), with (23.2) forbidding rotation and (23.3) omitted.
Explicitly assumes that a return to quiescence is possible, deferring the backscatter question.

sections.title: Characteristic hypersurfaces of Einstein's equations
sections.summary: Notes that the field equations are hyperbolic (wave equations in a suitable linearized gauge), and that hyperbolic systems allow 'time-bomb' solutions that switch on suddenly, with influences travelling along bicharacteristics lying in characteristic hypersurfaces that act as wave fronts and where different solutions can join and Cauchy data fail. Using the Cauchy evolution form g^{00} g_{ab,00} = 2M_{ab} from Ch. 13, the second time derivatives are undetermined exactly when g^{00} = 0, which is the null-hypersurface condition. A null hypersurface's normal is null, hence tangent, so the surface touches the light cone and is ruled by null geodesics that are the bicharacteristics.
key_moves: Contrast hyperbolic with elliptic and parabolic equations via the existence of initially static solutions that later become dynamic.
Characterize characteristic surfaces as those on which the Cauchy problem is not solvable.
Read off g^{00} = 0 as the obstruction in (13.23) and recall from §17.1 that it makes x^0 = const null.
Normal of a null surface is null, hence lies in the surface; surface is tangent to the local light cone (Fig. 23.2).
Conclude that gravitational disturbances propagate along null geodesics, recovering the linearized picture non-linearly.

sections.title: Radiation coordinates
sections.summary: Introduces u = x^0 labelling a non-intersecting family of null hypersurfaces, with covariant normal l_a = ∂_a u null. Shows by a short covariant calculation that the integral curves of l^a are null geodesics with affine parameter (null rays). Chooses x^1 = r as a radial parameter along the rays and, assuming asymptotic flatness, uses the polar angles on the spheres at future null infinity to label rays. These Bondi (radiation) coordinates are valid only near scri+, because rays traced inward generally focus and cross.
key_moves: Normal covector l_a = δ_a^0 and its nullness (23.6).

Absolute derivative of dx^a/dρ = g^{ab}∂_b u; swap ∇_c∂_b u = ∇_b∂_c u by symmetry of the connection; recognise a gradient of g^{cd}∂_c u ∂_d u, which vanishes because every member of the family is null (23.9).
Coordinates: r along rays, θ and φ fixed on each ray by their values at scri+ (23.12).
Honest limitation: caustics inside the source region mean the chart is only asymptotic (Fig. 23.3).

sections.title: Bondi's radiating metric
sections.summary: Converts the coordinate construction into restrictions on the metric. Since the r-lines are the rays, l^a = g^{0a} is proportional to δ^a_1, giving g^{00} = g^{02} = g^{03} = 0, equivalently g_{11} = g_{12} = g_{13} = 0. Contrasts the Newman-Penrose affine choice (g_{01} = 1) with Bondi's luminosity-distance choice fixing the angular 2-metric determinant to r^4 sin^2θ so spheres of constant u and r have area 4πr^2. Axial symmetry removes φ dependence and reflection invariance kills the φ cross terms, leaving Bondi's metric with four functions V, U, β, γ of (u, r, θ). Reinterprets it as a 2+2 split in which the u = const surfaces are null, r = const surfaces timelike, U and β carry shift and V the lapse.
key_moves: Tangent to a ray is δ^a_1, so l^a = λδ^a_1 and l^a = g^{0a} give (23.13).
Inverse-metric zeros translate into covariant zeros (23.14), a matrix-inversion exercise.
Radial gauge choice: affine (NP) versus areal determinant condition (23.16).
Symmetry reductions (23.17)-(23.19).
Assemble (23.20) with an exponential parametrization chosen to keep signature manifest.
Translate into 2+2 language (link to §14.13, Fig. 14.9).

sections.title: The characteristic initial value problem
sections.summary: Sets up evolution from data on a null hypersurface. Bondi's split of the ten vacuum equations: three components vanish identically by symmetry, four main equations, one trivial equation, two supplementary conditions. A lemma parallel to constraint propagation in the Cauchy problem: if the main equations hold everywhere, the Bianchi identities make the trivial equation hold algebraically and make the supplementary conditions hold everywhere once they hold on one r = const surface. The main equations divide into one dynamical equation (the only one with a u derivative) and three hypersurface equations acting within a null cone. For analytic solutions, one prescribes γ on N_0, solves the hypersurface equations for β, U, V, uses the dynamical equation for γ_{,u}, steps to the neighbouring cone and repeats; integration functions, including the news, are postponed.
key_moves: Lemma as the characteristic analogue of constraint preservation, with the roles of constraints played by the trivial and supplementary equations.
Further split (23.26)-(23.27): dynamical versus hypersurface.
Marching algorithm N_0 -> N_1 -> ... (Fig. 23.4).
Flag that neglected integration functions will matter.

sections.title: News and mass loss
sections.summary: Imposes asymptotic fall-off (23.28) and names the BMS group of form-preserving transformations as the asymptotic analogue of the Poincare group. Adds Bondi's outgoing condition (23.29), modelled on Sommerfeld's, while noting it cannot exclude weak incoming radiation. Expands γ, β, U, V in 1/r, introducing n, q, d, M; records the dynamical and (exact) supplementary equations. Data count: γ on N_0 (function of three variables), n_{,u} on scri+ (two variables), M and d on the cut N_0 ∩ scri+ (one variable). Since n_{,u} drives the evolution it is the news; M is the mass aspect, d and q dipole and quadrupole aspects; the angular average of M is the Bondi mass, matching ADM/Komar when stationary and Newton in the weak field. Integrating the M equation over the sphere gives the mass-loss formula: mass is lost if and only if there is news. The result is non-perturbative, coordinate independent (tied to the leading Weyl tensor), corresponds to the radiated power, holds in Sachs' general case with two news functions, and Bondi mass positivity was later proved.
key_moves: Asymptotic conditions (23.28) plus (23.29).
Expansions (23.30)-(23.31) with arbitrary functions n, q, d, M.
Supplementary equations (23.32)-(23.33) are exact because they need hold on only one r.
Free-data count (23.34)-(23.36) laid out on a Penrose diagram (Fig. 23.5).
Identify M with mass via static limit and define m(u) (23.37).
Multiply (23.32) by sin θ, integrate, drop the total-derivative term by axis regularity, obtain (23.38).
Theorem: mass loss iff news; interpret as radiated power without linearization.

sections.title: The Petrov classification
sections.summary: In vacuum the Riemann tensor equals the Weyl tensor, which is trace-free and has the Riemann symmetries. Viewed as a symmetric 6×6 matrix on bivector space it could be classified by eigenstructure; the extra symmetries reduce the problem to the root structure of a quartic, giving Petrov types I, II, D, III, N plus the conformally flat type O. Penrose's triangle arranges them by specialization; a spacetime's type is the most general type it attains, and types can only drop at special points. Type I is algebraically general, the rest special. Equivalently (Debever) one classifies principal null directions, of which there are between one and four, by their multiplicities. Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordstrom and Kerr are type D, plane waves type N; realistic sources are type I but become type N asymptotically, with curvature falling like n_{,uu}/r. Mentions Plebanski (Ricci) and Karlhede classifications.
key_moves: Vacuum reduction C_abcd = R_abcd via (23.39).
Pair symmetries -> 6×6 symmetric matrix; extra symmetries (23.40) and cyclic identity reduce sextic to quartic.
Table 23.1 (root multiplicities, eigenvector counts) and Fig. 23.6 hierarchy.
Debever theorem and Table 23.2 (PND coincidences).
Assign known solutions to types; Bondi solution type I with asymptotic type N.

sections.title: The peeling theorem
sections.summary: Gives physical meaning to the algebra. Sachs expanded the curvature of an outgoing linearized wave in an affine parameter along rays: the 1/r term is type N, 1/r^2 type III, 1/r^3 type II, 1/r^4 type I (with the 0 subscript meaning parallel propagated along the ray). He then showed the same structure holds for asymptotically flat isolated radiating systems in full GR: far out the four principal null directions coincide along the ray, and moving inward they separate one by one. Szekeres' test-particle analysis: type N squeezes and stretches a ring transverse to the propagation direction; type III produces a planar distortion in a plane containing the propagation direction, tilted by 45°; type D stretches a sphere into a prolate ellipsoid along the propagation direction, the familiar Schwarzschild tidal effect (Coulomb-like). Types I and II give nothing simple.
key_moves: Expansion (23.41) with each order labelled by its Petrov type.
Extension from linearized to full non-linear isolated systems (Sachs).
Pictorial statement: principal null directions peel off inward (Fig. 23.7).
Physical reading via orthonormal triads and deformed rings/spheres (Figs 23.8-23.10), cross-linked to Fig. 21.2 and §17.10.

sections.title: The optical scalars
sections.summary: For an affinely parametrized null geodesic congruence defines expansion, twist and shear. Sachs' interpretation: an object in the beam casts a shadow on a nearby screen whose size, rotation and distortion over distance dr are set by θ, ω and |σ|, independent of screen velocity. Shear is singled out by the Goldberg-Sachs theorem: a vacuum spacetime is algebraically special exactly when it has a shear-free null geodesic congruence; in isolated systems the news is related to shear. Petrov types, optical scalars and Killing vectors are the main invariant tools for finding exact solutions (all vacuum type D solutions are known) though many solutions remain poorly understood or pathological. Finally, the Ricci identity on l^a yields propagation equations such as the complex null Raychaudhuri equation, key to singularity theorems.
key_moves: Rescale l^a to affine form (exercise 23.10).
Define θ, ω, |σ| from symmetric, antisymmetric and trace parts of l_{a;b}.
Shadow-on-a-screen picture (Fig. 23.11).
Goldberg-Sachs theorem links congruence kinematics to Petrov type.
Status report on exact solutions classified by these tools.
Ricci identity (23.42) -> propagation equation for z = -θ + iω (23.44).

sections.title: Exercises and further reading
sections.summary: Eleven exercises: cylindrical symmetry and its non-rotating canonical form, deriving the Bondi metric conditions and line element, sphere area, the connection of the Bondi metric, proving the Bianchi lemma, Ricci components and the integration schema, the mass-loss derivation with axis regularity, the 6×6 matrix view of Weyl, affine rescaling of a null congruence, and the expansion of the Bondi congruence. Further reading points to Wald and Stewart for the Bondi metric, the original Bondi-van der Burg-Metzner paper, and Ludvigsen for optical scalars.
key_moves: Exercises supply the calculations the text quotes (23.3, 23.5-23.8).
Reading list separates advanced texts from the readable original paper.

concepts.name: radiating isolated source
concepts.definition: A bounded matter distribution in an otherwise empty, asymptotically flat spacetime that is stationary for all early times, emits gravitational radiation for a finite interval, and is stationary again afterwards; used to test whether radiation carries away mass-energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by doubts about linearized theory and by the unphysical, source-free nature of exact plane waves; drawn as a world tube with outgoing radiation bands and a smaller final mass.
concepts.notes: The assumption that the source can become quiescent again is explicitly not justified; backscatter could in principle keep it ringing.

concepts.name: energy transfer by gravitational waves
concepts.definition: Whether gravitational waves remove mass-energy from the body that emits them; the book takes this, not the mere existence of wave solutions, as the test of whether gravitational radiation is radiation in the same sense as light.
concepts.how_introduced: Set in bold in the opening paragraph as the reason to study bounded sources rather than source-free exact waves; it becomes the target proved by the Bondi mass-loss formula in §23.6, where the rate of mass decrease is identified with the radiated power dE/dt.
concepts.notes: Unlike the §21.9 flux formula, the non-linear result does not need a weak field.

concepts.name: non-linearity of the gravitational field
concepts.definition: The Einstein equations are non-linear in the metric, so solutions do not superpose and effects absent in the linearized theory (e.g. singularity formation from colliding plane waves, wave self-interaction) can occur.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening argument for why linearized conclusions about energy transport need independent confirmation.

concepts.name: axial symmetry
concepts.definition: Existence of a spacelike Killing vector ∂/∂φ with closed circular orbits, so the metric in adapted coordinates is unchanged under φ -> φ + const and its components do not depend on φ. Bondi also asks that this Killing vector be hypersurface orthogonal, which is the geometric form of the no-rotation condition that the discrete reflection φ -> -φ enforces.
concepts.how_introduced: The next simplest symmetry after the spherical and two-Killing-vector cases; imposed on the radiation coordinates and yielding ∂g_ab/∂φ = 0.

concepts.name: azimuthal reflection symmetry
concepts.definition: Invariance of the metric under φ -> -φ. Because a rotation would single out a sense of circulation about the axis, this symmetry excludes rotation; in adapted coordinates it forces all cross terms between dφ and the other coordinate differentials to vanish.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as (23.2) with a 'why?' prompt to the reader, then turned into g_03 = g_13 = g_23 = 0 in §23.4.
concepts.notes: The book leaves the 'why?' unanswered: under φ -> -φ a term like g_03 du dφ changes sign, and angular momentum about the axis flips sign, so invariance requires both to vanish.

concepts.name: hyperbolic system of field equations
concepts.definition: The vacuum Einstein equations, suitably gauge-fixed, form a hyperbolic system whose solutions propagate at finite speed along characteristics, unlike elliptic or parabolic systems.
concepts.how_introduced: Seen most easily in the linearized theory where a gauge reduces them to wave equations; used to motivate searching for wave fronts.

concepts.name: time-bomb solution
concepts.definition: A solution of a hyperbolic system that is exactly static up to some moment and then becomes dynamic, possible because data can be joined continuously across characteristic surfaces; elliptic and parabolic equations forbid this.
concepts.how_introduced: Borrowed from Bondi to dramatize the special character of hyperbolic equations.

concepts.name: characteristic hypersurface
concepts.definition: A hypersurface on which Cauchy data do not determine the normal (second) derivatives of the field, so distinct solutions can meet continuously across it; for Einstein's equations these are exactly the null hypersurfaces.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the Cauchy evolution equations (13.23): the coefficient g^{00} of g_{ab,00} vanishes precisely on null surfaces x^0 = const.

concepts.name: bicharacteristics
concepts.definition: The privileged curves lying in characteristic hypersurfaces along which disturbances propagate; for Einstein's equations they are the null geodesic generators of the null hypersurfaces.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in §23.2 and identified in §23.3 as integral curves of l^a = g^{ab}∂_b u, proven geodesic by (23.9).

concepts.name: null hypersurface
concepts.definition: A hypersurface whose normal vector is null; the normal therefore also lies in the surface, the surface is everywhere tangent to the local light cone, and it is generated by null geodesics.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from §17.1 via g^{00} = 0 and pictured as a cone ruled by rays with tangent-and-normal vector l^a (Fig. 23.2).

concepts.name: null rays
concepts.definition: For a family of null hypersurfaces u = const, the curves with tangent l^a = g^{ab}∂_b u satisfy l^b∇_b l^a = 0: they are null geodesics and the parameter along them is affine.
concepts.how_introduced: Proven by taking the absolute derivative of the tangent, using metric compatibility, the symmetry ∇_c∂_b u = ∇_b∂_c u, and the vanishing gradient of the norm of ∂u.

concepts.name: affine parameter
concepts.definition: A parameter along a geodesic for which the geodesic equation takes the form with zero right-hand side, fixed up to linear changes; Newman and Penrose used an affine parameter as the radial coordinate, giving g_01 = g^01 = 1.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the parameter ρ in (23.9) and as the alternative to Bondi's areal r in §23.4; Sachs' peeling expansion uses it.

concepts.name: radiation coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates adapted to outgoing null hypersurfaces: u (retarded time) labels the null hypersurfaces, r is a radial parameter along each null ray, and θ, φ label rays by the polar angles of the point where they reach future null infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Constructed step by step from the characteristic analysis; shown with a cone of rays capped by a sphere at scri+ and with caustics inside (Fig. 23.3).
concepts.notes: Only valid in a neighbourhood of scri+ because the rays generally focus and cross further in.

concepts.name: asymptotic flatness
concepts.definition: The metric approaches the Minkowski metric as one goes to large distances along outgoing null rays, with specified fall-off rates for the corrections.
concepts.how_introduced: First as g_ab -> η_ab (23.11), later strengthened to the fall-off conditions (23.28) needed for the 1/r expansion.

concepts.name: future null infinity
concepts.definition: The boundary of the conformally compactified spacetime reached by outgoing null rays as r -> ∞ at fixed retarded time; radiation is read off there, and angles on its cross-sections label rays.
concepts.how_introduced: Used without re-derivation (from the Penrose-diagram chapter) as the place where coordinates and news data are defined (Figs 23.3, 23.5).

concepts.name: luminosity distance parameter
concepts.definition: Bondi's choice of radial coordinate along rays fixed by demanding that the determinant of the angular 2-metric equal r^4 sin^2θ, so that each u = const, r = const 2-surface has area 4πr^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the alternative to the Newman-Penrose affine choice; its geometric meaning (sphere area) is checked in Exercise 23.4.

concepts.name: Bondi radiating metric
concepts.definition: The general axisymmetric, non-rotating line element in radiation coordinates, containing four free functions V, U, β, γ of (u, r, θ): ds^2 = (V e^{2β}/r - U^2 r^2 e^{2γ}) du^2 + 2e^{2β} du dr + 2U r^2 e^{2γ} du dθ - r^2(e^{2γ}dθ^2 + e^{-2γ} sin^2θ dφ^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by stacking the ray conditions, the areal gauge and the two symmetries on a general metric; interpreted in 2+2 language.
concepts.notes: γ carries the single radiative degree of freedom allowed by the symmetry; V/r -> 1 - 2M/r reproduces Schwarzschild-like behaviour.

concepts.name: 2+2 formalism
concepts.definition: Splitting spacetime into a two-parameter family of spacelike 2-surfaces and the 2-dimensional orthogonal directions, with lapse- and shift-like functions describing how neighbouring 2-surfaces are connected.
concepts.how_introduced: Bondi's metric is presented as an instance: 2-surfaces S_{u,r} with metric r^2(e^{2γ}dθ^2 + e^{-2γ}sin^2θ dφ^2), null u-surfaces, timelike r-surfaces, U and β as shifts, V as lapse.

concepts.name: characteristic initial value problem
concepts.definition: Posing data for the field equations on a null hypersurface (plus suitable data at its boundary, here at null infinity) rather than on a spacelike Cauchy surface, and evolving from one null hypersurface to the next.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the natural replacement for the Cauchy problem once characteristic surfaces are known to be wave fronts; organized by Bondi's grouping of the equations.

concepts.name: Bondi hierarchy of field equations
concepts.definition: Bondi's partition of the ten vacuum Ricci equations for the axisymmetric metric: three identically satisfied by symmetry (R_03, R_13, R_23), four main equations (R_11, R_12, R_22, R_33), one trivial (R_01) and two supplementary conditions (R_00, R_02).
concepts.how_introduced: Listed as (23.22)-(23.25) and then justified by the Bianchi lemma.

concepts.name: contracted Bianchi identities
concepts.definition: The identities ∇_b G^{ab} = 0, which here imply that if the main equations hold everywhere then the trivial equation holds algebraically and the supplementary conditions hold everywhere provided they hold on one r = const surface.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as an analogue of the Cauchy-problem theorem that constraints preserved by evolution need only be imposed initially; proof deferred to Exercise 23.6.
concepts.notes: Because they need hold on only one value of r, the supplementary equations can be imposed exactly at scri+, which is why (23.32)-(23.33) are exact.

concepts.name: hypersurface equations
concepts.definition: Three of the four main equations (the rr and rθ Ricci components together with the trace of the angular block) that involve only derivatives inside a single null hypersurface u = const; they act like radial ODE constraints that fix β, U and V once γ is known on that hypersurface.
concepts.how_introduced: Split out of the main equations to reveal the marching algorithm.

concepts.name: dynamical equation
concepts.definition: The single main equation R_33 = 0 containing a u derivative; it gives γ_{,u} on a null hypersurface and so propagates data to the next one.
concepts.how_introduced: Paired with the hypersurface equations in the integration schema.

concepts.name: null-cone integration schema
concepts.definition: Prescribe γ on an initial null hypersurface N_0; integrate the hypersurface equations for β, U, V; use the dynamical equation for γ_{,u}; thereby obtain γ on the neighbouring null hypersurface N_1; repeat.
concepts.how_introduced: Described for analytic solutions and drawn as two nested cones with labels for what is prescribed and what is determined (Fig. 23.4).

concepts.name: asymptotic expansion in 1/r
concepts.definition: Expanding each metric function in inverse powers of the areal radius along outgoing rays, keeping only as many orders as needed, so that the field equations become algebraic and differential relations among coefficient functions of (u, θ).
concepts.how_introduced: Required after the integration schema leaves functions of integration unidentified; yields n, q, d, M.

concepts.name: BMS group
concepts.definition: The group of coordinate transformations preserving the Bondi form of the metric and its asymptotic fall-off conditions; it is the asymptotic symmetry group of isolated radiating systems, playing the role the Poincare group plays in special relativity.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in passing after the asymptotic conditions (23.28).
concepts.notes: Beyond the text: it is infinite-dimensional, containing supertranslations in addition to Lorentz transformations.

concepts.name: outgoing radiation condition
concepts.definition: Bondi's requirement that ∂(r^2 γ)/∂r -> 0 as r -> ∞ at fixed u, intended to exclude radiation arriving from past null infinity; it turns out not to exclude sufficiently weak incoming radiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Justified by analogy with the Sommerfeld condition for electromagnetic waves.

concepts.name: news function
concepts.definition: The retarded-time derivative n_{,u}(u, θ) of the coefficient n of 1/r in γ; it is free data specified on future null infinity that alone drives the evolution, vanishes for stationary systems, and whose square gives the mass loss rate.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified by counting free data: after γ on N_0 and M, d on the initial cut, only n_{,u} remains to control how the solution changes.
concepts.notes: In general (Sachs) there are two news functions for the two polarizations; the news is related to the shear of outgoing null congruences at scri+.

concepts.name: mass aspect
concepts.definition: The function M(u, θ) appearing in V = r - 2M + O(1/r), whose angular average gives the Bondi mass; in stationary periods it reduces to the mass parameter.
concepts.how_introduced: Named after a coordinate transformation in a static period relates M to known physical parameters.

concepts.name: dipole aspect
concepts.definition: The function d(u, θ) in the r^{-3} term of U, related in static and weak-field limits to the Newtonian dipole moment.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as an arbitrary function in the expansion of U, named by comparison with the static case.

concepts.name: quadrupole aspect
concepts.definition: The function q(u, θ) in the r^{-3} term of γ, related in static and weak-field limits to the Newtonian quadrupole moment; its u derivative is fixed by the dynamical equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Named by comparison with the static case.

concepts.name: Bondi mass
concepts.definition: The total mass-energy of an isolated system measured at a cut u = const of future null infinity, given in the axisymmetric case by m(u) = ½∫_0^π M(u, θ) sin θ dθ; it agrees with the ADM and Komar masses for stationary spacetimes and with Newtonian mass in the weak-field limit.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as the angular average of the mass aspect; its physical meaning is supported by agreement with other mass definitions rather than derived.

concepts.name: Bondi mass-loss formula
concepts.definition: For an asymptotically flat isolated system the Bondi mass obeys dm/du = -½∫_0^π (n_{,u})^2 sin θ dθ ≤ 0, so the mass is constant exactly when there is no news and strictly decreases when there is; the loss equals the energy radiated in gravitational waves, with no weak-field approximation.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by multiplying the exact supplementary equation for M_{,u} by sin θ, integrating over θ, and discarding the total-derivative term using regularity on the axis.

concepts.name: positivity of Bondi mass
concepts.definition: For an asymptotically flat spacetime obeying the dominant energy condition, the Bondi mass is non-negative, so a radiating system cannot radiate away more than its mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as a natural worry once mass can decrease; credited to Ludvigsen and Vickers (1981) without proof.

concepts.name: two news functions
concepts.definition: Without axial and reflection symmetry the outgoing radiation is described by two news functions, one per gravitational polarization, and the mass-loss result holds with both contributing.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as Sachs' generalization of Bondi's work.

concepts.name: Weyl tensor
concepts.definition: The trace-free part of the Riemann tensor, with the same index symmetries as Riemann and all contractions vanishing; in vacuum it equals the Riemann tensor and it carries the free gravitational field.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled via (6.88) to justify classifying vacuum curvature algebraically.

concepts.name: Petrov classification
aliases: algebraic classification of the Weyl tensor
concepts.definition: Classification of the Weyl tensor at a point by the multiplicity structure of the roots of an associated quartic (equivalently of its principal null directions): type I (four distinct), II (one double), D (two double), III (one triple), N (one quadruple), plus type O where the Weyl tensor vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as eigen-analysis of the Weyl tensor as a 6×6 symmetric matrix on bivectors, with the extra symmetries reducing the problem to a quartic; summarized in Table 23.1.

concepts.name: Penrose specialization diagram
concepts.definition: The triangular arrangement of Petrov types with arrows pointing to more degenerate types: I -> II, I -> D, II -> D, II -> III, II -> N, D -> N, D -> O, III -> N, N -> O.
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn as Fig. 23.6; used to define the type of a spacetime as the least special type attained and to say types can only become more special at special points.

concepts.name: algebraically general and special spacetimes
concepts.definition: A vacuum spacetime is algebraically general if its Weyl tensor is Petrov type I (four distinct principal null directions) and algebraically special otherwise (at least two coincide).
concepts.how_introduced: Defined immediately after the hierarchy; later tied to shear-free congruences by Goldberg-Sachs.

concepts.name: principal null directions
concepts.definition: Null vectors l^a satisfying l_[a R_b]ef[c l_d] l^e l^f = 0 (with the Weyl tensor in place of Riemann off vacuum). Where the Weyl tensor is non-zero there are at least one and at most four of them at each point, and the pattern of their coincidences fixes the Petrov type; in type O the condition is empty and every null direction qualifies.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced via Debever's equivalent approach; Table 23.2 gives coincidence patterns [1111], [211], [22], [31], [4].

concepts.name: Plebanski classification
concepts.definition: An algebraic classification of the (trace-free) Ricci tensor that complements the Petrov classification of the Weyl tensor in non-vacuum spacetimes.
concepts.how_introduced: One-sentence mention.

concepts.name: Karlhede classification
concepts.definition: A complete invariant classification of a spacetime via the Weyl tensor and its covariant derivatives computed in a canonically fixed frame, used to decide whether two metrics are equivalent.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the full extension of algebraic classification, pointing back to the equivalence problem.

concepts.name: peeling theorem
concepts.definition: Along an outgoing null geodesic with affine parameter r in an asymptotically flat radiating spacetime, the curvature falls off as N/r + III/r^2 + II/r^3 + I/r^4 + O(r^{-5}), where the coefficient of r^{-k} has Petrov type with the ray direction as a principal null direction of multiplicity 5 - k; far away the field is type N and principal null directions separate as one moves inward.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated first for Sachs' linearized retarded waves and then for full isolated systems; visualized with bundles of arrows peeling apart (Fig. 23.7).
concepts.notes: The r^{-5} coefficient I'_0 is different in kind: its single principal null direction is not along the ray, so it carries no peeling structure. Sachs also found that algebraically special fields do not admit an expansion as general as (23.41). The text presents peeling as holding for Bondi-Sachs asymptotics; later work (beyond the text) shows it can fail for generic physically reasonable initial data.

concepts.name: wave zone
concepts.definition: The far region along outgoing rays where the 1/r, type N part of the curvature dominates and the field looks locally like a plane wave.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to phrase the peeling statement (start in the wave zone, move inward).

concepts.name: Szekeres test-particle interpretation
concepts.definition: Reading off the physical effect of a Petrov-type curvature field from the relative accelerations of a ring or sphere of free test particles in an adapted orthonormal spatial triad.
concepts.how_introduced: Applied to types N, III and D with a picture for each (Figs 23.8-23.10); types I and II give no simple picture.

concepts.name: transverse wave
concepts.definition: A type N curvature field distorts a ring of test particles only in the plane perpendicular to the propagation direction, stretching along one axis and squeezing along the orthogonal one.
concepts.how_introduced: Szekeres' label; linked back to the linearized ring distortion of Fig. 21.2.

concepts.name: longitudinal wave component
concepts.definition: A type III curvature field produces a planar distortion of a ring in a plane that contains the propagation direction, with the stretching axis at 45° to that direction.
concepts.how_introduced: Szekeres' label; drawn as a tilted ellipse (Fig. 23.9).

concepts.name: Coulomb-type field
concepts.definition: A type D curvature field deforms a sphere of test particles into a prolate ellipsoid elongated along the distinguished direction and compressed transversely, as for tidal forces on an observer falling radially into a Schwarzschild black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Szekeres' electromagnetic analogy; tied to §17.10 (Fig. 23.10).

concepts.name: null geodesic congruence
concepts.definition: A family of null geodesics filling a region with exactly one through each point, described by its tangent field l^a, which can always be rescaled so that l^a_{;b} l^b = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Starting object of §23.9; rescaling is Exercise 23.10.

concepts.name: optical scalars
concepts.definition: Three scalars built from the covariant derivative of an affinely parametrized null congruence that describe how an infinitesimal cross-section of the beam grows (expansion θ), rotates (twist ω) and distorts (shear |σ|) along the rays.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by formulas and interpreted through Sachs' shadow picture (Fig. 23.11).

concepts.name: expansion of a null congruence
concepts.definition: θ = ½ l^a_{;a}: the fractional rate of change of the linear size of a small shadow cast by the beam per unit affine distance.
concepts.how_introduced: One of the three optical scalars; Exercise 23.11 computes it for the Bondi congruence.

concepts.name: twist of a null congruence
concepts.definition: ω, built from the antisymmetric part of l_{a;b}: the rate at which the shadow rotates per unit affine distance; it vanishes for hypersurface-orthogonal congruences such as the generators of u = const.
concepts.how_introduced: One of the three optical scalars.

concepts.name: shear of a null congruence
concepts.definition: |σ|, built from the trace-free symmetric part of l_{a;b}: the rate at which a circular shadow is distorted into an ellipse per unit affine distance; physically the most important scalar because of the Goldberg-Sachs theorem and its link to news.
concepts.how_introduced: One of the three optical scalars, singled out afterwards.

concepts.name: Sachs shadow interpretation
concepts.definition: Operational meaning of the optical scalars: a small opaque object in the null beam casts a shadow on a screen a small affine distance dr away that is enlarged by θ dr, rotated by ω dr and sheared by |σ| dr, and this shadow is the same for screens with any velocity at that point.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as Sachs' result immediately after the definitions, with a three-panel figure.

concepts.name: Goldberg-Sachs theorem
concepts.definition: A vacuum spacetime is algebraically special (has a repeated principal null direction) if and only if it admits a shear-free null geodesic congruence (tangent to the repeated direction).
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the reason shear is physically the most important optical scalar; used to organize exact-solution searches by expansion and twist.

concepts.name: null Raychaudhuri equation
concepts.definition: The propagation equation along an affinely parametrized null congruence for the complex quantity z = -θ + iω: Dz/Dr = z^2 + |σ|^2 + ½R_ab l^a l^b; its real part shows that shear and positive R_ab l^a l^b drive focusing.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in outline from the Ricci identity applied to l^a; flagged as central to singularity theorems.

concepts.name: Ricci identity
concepts.definition: For a vector field, the difference of second covariant derivatives taken in opposite orders equals a contraction of the Riemann tensor with the vector: l^a_{;bc} - l^a_{;cb} = R^a_{dcb} l^d in this book's convention.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked without proof to derive propagation equations for the optical scalars.

concepts.name: ADM mass
concepts.definition: The total mass of an asymptotically flat spacetime defined at spatial infinity from the asymptotic metric; conserved and shown positive, unlike the Bondi mass which can decrease.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled as a consistency check for the Bondi mass and as the positivity precedent.

concepts.name: Komar mass
concepts.definition: A mass defined for stationary spacetimes as a surface integral of the derivative of the timelike Killing vector; coincides with the Bondi mass during stationary epochs.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled only as a consistency check.

key_equations.name: Axial symmetry
key_equations.meaning: The metric is invariant under rotations about the symmetry axis.

key_equations.name: Azimuthal reflection
key_equations.meaning: Reflection invariance that rules out rotation of the source.

key_equations.name: Equatorial reflection (not used)
key_equations.meaning: Optional extra symmetry through the equatorial plane; discarded since it does not simplify much.

key_equations.name: Cauchy evolution equations (recalled 13.23)
key_equations.meaning: Second time derivatives of the spatial metric can be solved for only if g^{00} ≠ 0; the failure g^{00} = 0 characterizes wave fronts.
key_equations.symbols: M_{αβ} terms with at most first time derivatives; Greek indices spatial

key_equations.name: Null hypersurface family
key_equations.meaning: Retarded-time coordinate whose level sets are non-intersecting null hypersurfaces.

key_equations.name: Normal covector
key_equations.meaning: Gradient of u is the normal to the u = const surfaces.

key_equations.name: Nullness of the normal
key_equations.meaning: The surfaces are null, so the normal is also tangent to them; equivalently g^{00} = 0.

key_equations.name: Bicharacteristic curves
key_equations.meaning: Rays are integral curves of the raised normal.

key_equations.name: Rays are affinely parametrized null geodesics
key_equations.meaning: Uses metric compatibility, the symmetry ∇_c∂_b u = ∇_b∂_c u of a torsion-free connection, and the vanishing of the gradient of l_a l^a (null on every surface of the family).

key_equations.name: Radial coordinate
key_equations.meaning: r is a parameter along each null ray.

key_equations.name: Asymptotic flatness
key_equations.meaning: Metric tends to Minkowski along outgoing rays.

key_equations.name: Angular ray labels
key_equations.meaning: Polar angles on the spheres at scri+ label the rays.

key_equations.name: Ray tangent
key_equations.meaning: Tangent to r-lines must be proportional to l^a, which is the 0-row of the inverse metric.

key_equations.name: Contravariant ray conditions
key_equations.meaning: Consequence of the r-lines being the null rays.

key_equations.name: Covariant ray conditions
key_equations.meaning: Equivalent covariant statement, obtained by inverting a symmetric 4×4 matrix with the zeros of (23.13).

key_equations.name: Newman-Penrose affine gauge
key_equations.meaning: If r is taken affine, λ = 1.

key_equations.name: Bondi areal (luminosity) gauge
key_equations.meaning: Fixes r so that u, r = const spheres have area 4πr^2.

key_equations.name: Axial symmetry on metric
key_equations.meaning: No φ dependence.

key_equations.name: Reflection invariance on metric
key_equations.meaning: No cross terms between dφ and du, dr, dθ.

key_equations.name: Bondi radiating metric
key_equations.meaning: General axisymmetric non-rotating metric in radiation coordinates with signature (+,-,-,-).
key_equations.symbols: V, U, β, γ free functions

key_equations.name: Free functions
key_equations.meaning: Four functions of three variables remain after all gauge and symmetry choices.

key_equations.name: 2-surface metric
key_equations.meaning: Metric on S_{u,r} in the 2+2 interpretation; determinant r^4 sin^2θ independent of γ.

key_equations.name: Symmetry conditions
key_equations.meaning: Vanish identically because of the symmetries.

key_equations.name: Main equations
key_equations.meaning: The equations that must be solved everywhere.

key_equations.name: Trivial equation
key_equations.meaning: Holds algebraically once the main equations hold.

key_equations.name: Supplementary conditions
key_equations.meaning: Need only be imposed on one r = const surface.

key_equations.name: Dynamical equation
key_equations.meaning: Only main equation with a u derivative; propagates γ to the next null hypersurface.

key_equations.name: Hypersurface equations
key_equations.meaning: Equations internal to a null hypersurface determining β, U, V from γ.

key_equations.name: Asymptotic fall-off
key_equations.meaning: Strengthened asymptotic flatness conditions; transformations preserving these and (23.20) form the BMS group.

key_equations.name: Bondi outgoing condition
key_equations.meaning: Sommerfeld-like attempt to exclude incoming radiation; too weak to exclude weak incoming waves.

key_equations.name: Expansion of γ
key_equations.meaning: No 1/r^2 term; n(u, θ) carries the radiation, q(u, θ) the quadrupole aspect.
key_equations.symbols: n, q functions of (u, θ); n is c in Bondi's original notation

key_equations.name: Hypersurface-equation results
key_equations.meaning: β, U, V determined from γ up to integration functions d and M.
key_equations.symbols: d dipole aspect, M mass aspect; comma-2 is ∂_θ

key_equations.name: Dynamical equation at leading order
key_equations.meaning: Evolution of the quadrupole aspect.

key_equations.name: Mass-aspect evolution
key_equations.meaning: Exact supplementary result: mass aspect changes by minus the news squared plus a total angular derivative term.

key_equations.name: Dipole-aspect evolution
key_equations.meaning: Second exact supplementary result.

key_equations.name: Free data
key_equations.meaning: One function of three variables, one of two, two of one; everything else follows.

key_equations.name: Bondi mass
key_equations.meaning: Angular average of the mass aspect; total mass at a cut of scri+.

key_equations.name: Bondi mass-loss formula
key_equations.meaning: Mass is non-increasing and strictly decreases whenever news is non-zero; mass loss iff news.

key_equations.name: Weyl tensor decomposition
key_equations.meaning: Weyl tensor as Riemann minus its trace parts; in vacuum C = R.

key_equations.name: Trace-free property
key_equations.meaning: All contractions of Weyl vanish.

key_equations.name: Weyl symmetries (Ex. 23.9)
key_equations.meaning: Pair antisymmetry and pair exchange symmetry let C act as a symmetric 6×6 matrix on bivectors; the cyclic identity and tracelessness reduce the classification to a quartic.

key_equations.name: Principal null direction condition (Debever)
key_equations.meaning: Defines between one and four principal null directions at each point of a vacuum spacetime (C replaces R otherwise).

key_equations.name: Asymptotic curvature of Bondi solution
key_equations.meaning: Leading curvature is type N and set by the u derivative of the news.

key_equations.name: Peeling expansion
key_equations.meaning: Successive orders in affine distance are of Petrov types N, III, II, I; subscript 0 means parallel propagated along the ray.

key_equations.name: Affinely parametrized null congruence
key_equations.meaning: Achievable by rescaling l^a (Exercise 23.10).

key_equations.name: Optical scalars
key_equations.meaning: Expansion, twist and shear of the congruence.
key_equations.symbols: θ here is expansion, not the polar angle

key_equations.name: Ricci identity
key_equations.meaning: Starting point for optical scalar propagation equations.

key_equations.name: Complex expansion-twist
key_equations.meaning: Combines expansion and twist into one complex scalar.

key_equations.name: Null Raychaudhuri (Sachs) equation
key_equations.meaning: Real part: θ_{,r} = -θ^2 + ω^2 - |σ|^2 - ½R_ab l^a l^b, so shear and matter focus the beam; imaginary part: ω_{,r} = -2θω.
key_equations.symbols: r affine parameter along the congruence

figures.label: Fig. 23.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: World-tube picture of a source whose mass after radiating is smaller than before.
figures.visual_description: Spacetime diagram with an upward 'Time' arrow at lower left. A vertical hatched strip is the source world tube, labelled m_1 in its lower part and m_2 in its upper part. Between two dashed arcs the tube tapers inward (the radiating episode). From that tapered section two diagonal bands run up-left and up-right at 45 degrees, each bounded by straight lines labelled 'Null hypersurface' and filled with wavy lines labelled 'Radiation'. Above the bands the tube continues narrower than below. A pointer labelled 'Source' marks the lower (wider) part of the tube.
figures.what_it_teaches: States the goal of the chapter before the mathematics: a static source radiates for a finite time along null cones and ends static with smaller mass.

redesign.idea: Radiating-source timeline: a 2D spacetime diagram where the learner draws or selects a news profile n_u(u) (e.g. a burst) and watches the world-tube width and a Bondi-mass readout m(u) drop exactly during the burst while radiation shells leave along 45-degree lines.
redesign.interaction: Drag control points of the news pulse amplitude and duration; the mass curve updates from m_u = -⟨n_u^2⟩ and the outgoing null bands shade by energy flux.

figures.label: Fig. 23.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: A null hypersurface drawn as a cone.
figures.visual_description: A cone opening upward, its apex cut off at the bottom, ruled by several straight generator lines. One generator carries an upward arrow labelled l^a. Left labels point to the surface ('Null hypersurface') and a generator ('Null geodesic (rays)'). Right labels: 'Tangent and normal vector' pointing at the arrow, and 'Surface everywhere tangent to local light cone' pointing at a tiny light cone drawn sitting on the surface.
figures.what_it_teaches: The normal to a null surface lies in the surface and runs along its generating null geodesics; the surface grazes each local light cone.

redesign.idea: 3D null-surface explorer: a surface in 2+1 Minkowski space whose tilt the learner can vary from spacelike through null to timelike, with local light cones drawn at sample points and the normal vector rendered.
redesign.interaction: Slider for surface slope; when null, the normal visibly slides into the surface and coincides with a generator, and the light cones become tangent.

figures.label: Fig. 23.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Construction of Bondi's radiation coordinates u, r, θ, φ.
figures.visual_description: Two long straight lines form a Λ shape, each labelled ℐ+ at its upper end. Between them a large horizontal ellipse (a 2-sphere at scri+) caps a funnel-shaped null hypersurface that narrows downward; its generators converge and cross near the bottom, where small cusps are drawn. Labels: 'θ, φ defined on S^2 label rays' (pointing at the ellipse), 'Null hypersurface u = constant', 'r radial parameter along null rays' (pointing at a generator), and 'Rays focus and cross in general' (pointing at the caustic region).
figures.what_it_teaches: Shows what each coordinate means and why the chart breaks down inside where rays form caustics.

redesign.idea: Coordinate builder: in a 3D compactified sketch, the learner picks a point on a sphere at scri+ (setting θ, φ), slides u to choose the null cone and r along the ray; a lensing mass in the middle can be switched on to show rays focusing and the coordinate grid tearing at caustics.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for u, r, θ, φ and source compactness; highlight region where the chart is single-valued.

figures.label: Fig. 23.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: How Bondi's equations are integrated from one null hypersurface to the next.
figures.visual_description: Two nearly coincident funnel surfaces sharing a pair of close ellipses at the top, labelled at the bottom 'N_0: u = u_0' and 'N_1: u = u_1 (= u_0 + du)'. A left label reads 'Prescribe γ on N_0'; a right label reads 'Main equations determine γ on N_1'.
figures.what_it_teaches: The characteristic evolution is a marching procedure: data on one null cone plus the equations give data on the next.

redesign.idea: Step-through algorithm animation: stacked null cones N_0, N_1, N_2 with a pipeline panel (γ -> hypersurface equations -> β, U, V -> dynamical equation -> γ_u -> next cone); a toy 1+1 characteristic wave equation actually runs underneath so the learner sees data advance.
redesign.interaction: Step button advances one cone; learner edits the initial γ profile and sees the evolved profiles on later cones.

figures.label: Fig. 23.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram showing where the free data of the characteristic problem are placed.
figures.visual_description: A diamond-shaped Penrose diagram with i+ at top, i- at bottom and i^0 at the right corner; the upper-right edge is labelled ℐ+ and lower-right edge ℐ-. A thin hatched spindle running vertically from i- to i+ is labelled 'Source'. A thin lens-shaped (edge-on ellipse) curve crossing the upper half of the diagram and labelled N_0 at the right represents the null hypersurface N_0 reaching out to ℐ+. Boxed labels on the left: 'γ' pointing to N_0, 'M d' pointing to the point where N_0 meets ℐ+, and 'n_{,0}' with lines to the portion of ℐ+ above that cut.
figures.what_it_teaches: Free data: a function of three variables on the null cone, a function of two on scri+ (the news), and two functions of one variable on the cut.

redesign.idea: Data-placement puzzle on a Penrose diagram: the learner drags data tokens (γ, news, M, d) to the region where they must be prescribed; correct placement lights up the domain of dependence that becomes determined, and changing the news on a stretch of scri+ recolours the future region it influences.
redesign.interaction: Drag-and-drop tokens, then scrub a cut u along scri+ with a readout of the Bondi mass.

figures.label: Fig. 23.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose's triangular diagram of Petrov types ordered by specialization.
figures.visual_description: Letters arranged in a triangle: I at the apex; II at middle-left and D at middle-right; III, N and 0 (type O) along the bottom row from left to right. Arrows: I to II, I to D, II to D (horizontal), II to III, II to N, D to N, D to 0, III to N and N to 0 (horizontal).
figures.what_it_teaches: Types become more degenerate along arrows; a solution's type is its least special one and can only move down the arrows at special points.

redesign.idea: Clickable Petrov lattice linked to principal-null-direction dots on a celestial sphere: clicking a type merges the corresponding PNDs; dragging PNDs together on the sphere moves the highlight down the arrows automatically.
redesign.interaction: Drag four PND markers on a sphere; the node for the resulting type lights and legal degeneration arrows animate.

figures.label: Fig. 23.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Peeling: principal null directions separating order by order in 1/r.
figures.visual_description: Four groups of arrows side by side. 'N r^-1': four parallel arrows pointing up and to the left. 'III r^-2': three parallel arrows up-left and one up-right. 'II r^-3': two parallel arrows up-left, one nearly vertical, one up-right. 'I r^-4': four arrows fanning out from a common base in different directions.
figures.what_it_teaches: Each order in the curvature expansion has the outgoing ray as a principal null direction with decreasing multiplicity; far away all four coincide.

redesign.idea: Peeling slider: a radial position slider along an outgoing ray from source to scri+; four PND arrows on a small sphere merge into one as r grows, while a stacked bar shows relative sizes of the N, III, II, I terms falling as 1/r, 1/r^2, 1/r^3, 1/r^4.
redesign.interaction: Drag r (log scale); arrows and bar heights update, with a readout of the dominant Petrov type.

figures.label: Fig. 23.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Distortion of a ring of test particles by a type N field.
figures.visual_description: A circle overlaid by an ellipse elongated vertically. Short arrows on the ring point outward at top and bottom and inward at left and right. At the centre a triad: e_2 points up, e_3 points down-right in the ring plane, and e_1 points out of the ring plane (drawn as a short oblique arrow), marking the propagation direction.
figures.what_it_teaches: Type N effects are transverse: stretching and squeezing only perpendicular to the propagation direction, like the linearized plane wave.

redesign.idea: Three-mode tidal lab (shared with Figs 23.9-23.10): a 3D cloud of free particles with a propagation arrow; choosing type N, III or D applies the corresponding tidal tensor and animates the particle displacements, with the option to rotate the camera.
redesign.interaction: Type selector, amplitude and phase sliders, camera orbit; overlay of principal stretch axes.

figures.label: Fig. 23.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: Distortion of a ring of test particles by a type III field.
figures.visual_description: A circle with an ellipse tilted about 45 degrees (long axis running from lower-left to upper-right). Arrows point outward near the ends of the long axis and inward near the ends of the short axis. Triad at centre: e_3 up, e_2 up-right, e_1 to the right; the distortion plane contains e_1.
